title: Bagna Cauda
subtitle: Warm Piedmontese anchovy and garlic dipping sauce with raw vegetables
excerpt: Bagna cauda is a warm dipping sauce from Piedmont made of olive oil, butter, garlic, and anchovies, kept warm over a small flame at the table while raw and lightly blanched vegetables are dipped into it. The name means hot bath in Piedmontese dialect. It is communal, seasonal, and one of the defining dishes of the Piedmontese table.
sourceNotes: Bagna cauda is a traditional Piedmontese dish, particularly associated with the Langhe and Monferrato areas of southern Piedmont. It is documented in multiple nineteenth-century Piedmontese cookery texts and is served at the Bagna Cauda Day festival held annually in Asti.

content.text: Bagna cauda is made in a small earthenware or metal pot (a fujot) that sits over a tea light or spirit burner at the table. The sauce is pungent with garlic and anchovy but becomes mellow and sweet with long, slow cooking. The vegetables are the centrepiece: a wide selection of raw cardoons, peppers, fennel, celery, radishes, and carrots alongside briefly blanched cauliflower, cabbage, and artichokes.

items.prepNote: broken into small florets, briefly blanched

content.text: Place {{garlic}} of sliced garlic in a small saucepan with {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil over the lowest possible heat. Cook very gently for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the garlic is completely soft but not coloured. The oil should barely simmer.

Add {{anchovies}} of anchovies and mash them into the oil with a wooden spoon. Continue cooking over a low heat for 5 more minutes until the anchovies have completely dissolved into the sauce and the mixture is smooth. Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} of butter until melted.

Transfer to a small pot suitable for keeping warm at the table over a tea light. Arrange all the prepared vegetables -- {{pepper-red}} peppers, {{fennel}} fennel, {{celery}} celery, {{carrot}} carrots, and blanched {{cauliflower}} cauliflower -- around the pot. Each person dips vegetables into the warm sauce. Replenish the pot with a little extra oil and butter if needed.

items.cause: The garlic was cooked too fast or over too high a heat.
items.fix: Bagna cauda must be cooked over the absolute lowest heat possible. The garlic should become sweet and soft without any browning at all. If your hob runs hot, use a heat diffuser.

items.cause: The butter was added to oil that was too hot.
items.fix: Remove from the heat, allow to cool slightly, then stir vigorously. A split bagna cauda can sometimes be brought back together. Next time add the butter off the heat.

content.text: Bagna cauda is the communal dish of the Piedmontese harvest. It is traditionally eaten in autumn and winter, when the wine grape harvest was finished and the new season's wine was available. The sauce is kept warm in individual earthenware pots (one per person) or a shared pot in the centre of the table. The dish requires conversation and time: there is no hurrying the garlic. In the Langhe hills, the sauce is sometimes finished with cream to mellow the sharpness of the anchovies.
